title: Badanekayi yennegai (stuffed brinjal)
servingLabel: half the curry; eat with rotti or rice
uses: 1 burner, lidded heavy pan and mixer
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: North Karnataka-style fresh-coconut and onion variant. Peanuts and sesame are essential here; this is not Tamil ennai kathirikai. Sauce water is a starting amount, adjusted by tenderness.

items.name: Small tender purple brinjals
items.note: whole tender baby brinjals; use weight, count varies

stepTemplates: Prepare. Rinse {{brinjal}} brinjals. Cut two crossing slits from the rounded end towards the stalk, keeping the crown joined. Inspect inside; discard damaged fruit. Hold in water while making the paste, then drain and pat dry.
Extract. Soften {{tamarind}} tamarind in {{soak}} warm water for 10 minutes. Squeeze and strain; retain the liquid, discard seeds or fibres.
Roast. In a dry pan on low heat, stir {{peanuts}} peanuts until nutty; roast {{sesame}} sesame separately until fragrant. Cool before grinding.

Grind. Powder the cooled nuts and seeds. Blend with {{coconut}} fresh coconut, {{cumin}} cumin, {{chilli}} chillies, {{ginger}} ginger and {{herb}} coriander, adding {{grind}} water gradually. Stop at a thick, spoonable paste.

Combine. Mix in {{onion}} onion, {{sambar}} sambar powder, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{jaggery}} jaggery, {{salt}} salt and enough tamarind liquid to keep the stuffing thick. Reserve remaining liquid. Do not taste uncooked spice paste to assess final seasoning.
Stuff. Gently ease paste into each slit without snapping the crown. Retain every spoon of leftover paste for the gravy.
Temper. Heat {{oil}} oil on medium in a heavy lidded pan. Add {{mustard}} mustard; when it crackles, add {{garlic}} garlic and {{leaves}} curry leaves carefully. Lower heat if garlic darkens.

Simmer. Set brinjals in one layer. Turn gently for 2–3 minutes. Add leftover stuffing, reserved tamarind liquid and {{simmer}} water. Cover and simmer gently for about 20–30 minutes; turn and scrape the base every few minutes.

Check. A knife should enter the thick flesh beside the crown easily. If firm or the gravy catches, add a small splash of water and cook longer. Stop when the flesh is soft and the sauce coats it; oil separation alone is not doneness. Adjust seasoning after cooking.

title: Khara pongal (ven pongal)
uses: 3 L stovetop pressure cooker, burner and small tempering pan
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: A rice-forward, softly mashed pongal. The estimated raw-start time includes natural pressure release and tempering. Confirm pressure-cooker availability before choosing this version.
stepTemplates: Roast and rinse. Pick over {{dal}} dal. Dry-roast on low until fragrant, not brown. Cool briefly; rinse with {{rice}} rice and drain.

Load. Add grains, {{water}} water, {{ginger}} ginger, {{cumin-cook}} cumin, {{hing}} hing and {{salt}} salt to the cooker. Follow its minimum liquid and foaming-food fill limits; never scale past those limits.

Pressure-cook. Close according to the manufacturer. The source gives roughly 11–12 minutes at pressure; cooker and dal age vary. Maintain the cooker’s required operating heat, then turn off. This is not a universal whistle count.
Release. Wait for pressure to fall naturally and the indicator to confirm zero pressure before opening. Allow roughly 10–20 minutes, longer if needed; never force the lid.

Texture. Both grains should mash readily. If still firm, add liquid if needed and cook further using the cooker instructions. Mash lightly; thin thick pongal with hot water until soft and spoonable, not separate like pulao.
Temper. In a small pan heat {{ghee}} ghee. Sizzle {{cumin}} cumin; add {{nuts}} cashews until pale gold, then {{pepper}} pepper and {{leaves}} curry leaves carefully. Stop before spices burn.
Finish. Stir the tempering into the hot grains. Rest loosely covered for 5 minutes; loosen with hot water if it thickens. Serve hot.

title: Kesari Bath (rava sweet)
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: A small-portion Karnataka sweet, not a high-protein meal or a weight-loss claim. This version uses the Dassana water/sugar ratio, not the richer Hebbar ratio.

items.name: Saffron
items.note: optional; omit for an uncoloured sweet

stepTemplates: Roast. Stir {{rava}} fine rava in a dry heavy pan on low for about 5–6 minutes, until fragrant without darkening. Transfer to a plate.
Nuts. Melt {{ghee-nut}} ghee in the pan. Fry {{nuts}} cashews until pale gold; lift onto a plate. Keep the ghee in the pan.
Liquid. Add {{water}} water cautiously, then {{sugar}} sugar and {{raisins}} raisins. Add {{saffron}} saffron if using. Stir until dissolved and bring to a gentle boil.
Combine. Reduce heat. Sprinkle in the roasted rava in several additions while stirring continuously with a long-handled spoon. Keep hands and face away from hot splashes.
Cook. Mix in {{ghee-finish}} ghee and {{cardamom}} cardamom. Cover and cook on the lowest heat for 3–4 minutes, stirring to prevent catching.
Check. The granules should be fully swollen with no hard pale centres. If gritty, add a little hot water and cook longer. Fold in the nuts and serve warm; it firms as it cools.

title: Cabbage pakoda (besan fritters)
sub: cabbage pakora · patta gobhi pakode · cabbage bhajiya
servingLabel: half the batch of small fritters
uses: 1 burner, deep frying pan, slotted spoon and oil thermometer
keeps: Cook for this meal; refrigerate promptly if saving any.
intro: Besan-only cabbage fritters. This is a fried snack, not a low-oil recipe. Nutrition assumes 20 g oil absorbed by the whole batch solely for estimation; actual uptake may differ substantially.

items.name: Neutral oil for the pan
items.note: pan quantity, not consumption; actual absorbed oil is unknown

stepTemplates: Prepare. Rinse vegetables and drain thoroughly. Finely shred {{cabbage}} cabbage; chop {{onion}} onion and {{chilli}} chilli. Keep water away from the hot-oil area.
Mix. Combine vegetables with {{besan}} besan, {{ginger}} ginger, {{herb}} coriander, {{turmeric}} turmeric, {{powder}} chilli powder and {{salt}} salt.

Hydrate. Add water a spoon at a time, up to {{water}} initially. Vegetables release moisture, so stop once a thick mixture clings to a spoon. It should drop in small mounds, not pour as a thin batter.
Heat oil. Use {{oil}} as a pan-size guide, enough for frying while keeping the deep pan well below half full. Heat on medium to about 180 °C. Never leave it unattended or add water to oil.
Test. Lower one small spoonful close to the oil surface using a dry spoon. It should rise with steady bubbles. Reduce heat if it darkens before the middle cooks; recheck temperature.

Fry. Add a few small, loose spoonfuls without crowding. Let the coating set, then turn gently. Fry until evenly golden; open the first fritter and check for a cooked, non-pasty centre and tender cabbage.
Finish. Lift with a slotted spoon and drain on kitchen paper. Let oil return to temperature before each batch; total time depends on pan size. Serve hot with a separately prepared chutney.

sources.title: Dassana’s Veg Recipes: cabbage pakoda
sources.scope: Primary besan-only batter, incremental water and cooked-centre checks; cup amounts converted to approximate weights. Optional sesame and hing omitted.

sources.title: Hebbar’s Kitchen: lachhedar cabbage pakoda
sources.scope: Compared batch frying and moisture control. Its three-flour dry mixture is a different variant; those flour ratios are not used here.
